check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene and clear introduction:

kids.x: Confirms name and age.
Explains the purpose of the consultation.

check.x: Uses plain language, empathy and appropriate non-verbal communication throughout, facing her and speaking towards her better ear.
History
Characterises the hearing loss:

kids.x: Sudden onset on waking two days ago, one ear only (left), constant, not fluctuating.
Severity: cannot make out words on the phone in the left ear.
Previous episodes or previous hearing problems.

check.x: Asks about associated ear symptoms:

kids.x: Unilateral tinnitus and aural fullness.
Otalgia, otorrhoea or itch.
Vertigo and imbalance (brief unsteadiness yesterday, now resolved).

check.x: Screens for stroke and central red flags: facial droop, limb weakness or numbness, speech, swallowing or visual disturbance, severe headache.
Explores possible causes:

kids.x: Recent upper respiratory infection.
Head trauma, barotrauma, loud noise exposure.
Ear history and surgery, and self-treatment (olive oil drops).

check.x: Asks about ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, chemotherapy, high-dose aspirin or NSAIDs).
Elicits medical history relevant to corticosteroid treatment and vascular risk:

kids.x: Type 2 diabetes, recognised as relevant to steroid use.
Hypertension.
Peptic ulcer disease and mental health history.

check.x: Takes a medication history and allergies.
Takes a family and social history (family hearing loss, mother's stroke, occupation, alcohol, smoking, earbud use).
Elicits ideas, concerns and expectations (wax or the cold; fear of stroke, tumour or permanent deafness; expects a flush or antibiotics).
Examination
Inspects the external ears and mastoids, and performs otoscopy of both canals and tympanic membranes.
Performs Weber and Rinne tests with a 512 Hz tuning fork, and a whisper or finger-rub test of each ear.
Examines the cranial nerves, including facial nerve function and eye movements, and looks for nystagmus.
Checks coordination and gait (finger-nose, gait, Romberg) and a head impulse test.
Asks for observations, including blood pressure and capillary blood glucose.
Interpretation
Normal otoscopy makes wax, otitis externa or media, and perforation unlikely.
Weber to the right with Rinne positive on both sides indicates a left sensorineural hearing loss.

Audiogram: left sensorineural loss of 40 to 70 dB with no air-bone gap, at least 30 dB worse than the right over three or more contiguous frequencies, with poor speech discrimination; with onset within 72 hours this confirms sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

Tympanometry type A confirms a normal middle ear (no effusion or conductive cause); HbA1c 7.4% is a little above the usual target of 7% or less, and steroids will worsen her glucose; normal kidney function.

Recognises sudden sensorineural hearing loss as time-critical, usually idiopathic, and names causes to exclude: a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma, posterior circulation stroke, and ototoxic, infective or autoimmune causes.
Management
Arranges urgent same-day contact with ENT or the local ENT pathway.
Starts a corticosteroid promptly, without waiting for the MRI:

kids.x: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily (72 mg for her 72 kg, capped at the local protocol's maximum of 60 to 75 mg) for about 7 days and then tapered, or 7 to 14 days in some protocols, per the local guideline or ENT advice.
Mentions intratympanic steroid as an ENT-led option, for example if oral steroids are contraindicated or as salvage.

check.x: Explains that MRI of the internal auditory canals is needed to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma, which can present as sudden hearing loss.
Explains that the MRI is still required even if her hearing improves with steroids, because improvement does not exclude a retrocochlear lesion.
Addresses MRI concerns:

kids.x: Screens for MRI safety (pacemaker, metal implants).
Acknowledges her claustrophobia and offers options (explanation, a support person, an anxiolytic if needed, discussion with radiology about a wider-bore scanner).

check.x: Explains why an ear flush and antibiotics are not indicated (no wax, no infection).
Addresses diabetes and steroid safety:

kids.x: Warns that steroids will raise her blood glucose.
Gives a plan for home glucose monitoring, especially in the afternoon, with early review or medication adjustment if readings run high.
Mentions other steroid adverse effects (insomnia, mood change, indigestion) and taking the tablets in the morning with food.

check.x: Explains the likely diagnosis and plan in plain language, and why waiting over the weekend is unsafe: earlier treatment gives a better chance of recovery.
Gives an honest prognosis: many people recover some or all of their hearing, the outcome is uncertain, and earlier treatment is better.
Safety netting
Tells her to go to the Emergency Department immediately or call 000 for vertigo, facial or limb weakness or numbness, speech or visual change, severe headache, or hearing loss in the other ear.
Arranges follow-up: ENT review, a repeat audiogram to measure the response, a glucose check within a few days of starting steroids, the MRI result, and hearing rehabilitation if the loss persists.

desc: This station involves a focused history and ear and neurological examination of a woman with sudden hearing loss in one ear, then interpreting her audiogram, tympanometry and recent bloods, and explaining the urgent management: same-day ENT contact, prompt steroids with a diabetes plan, an MRI to exclude a retrocochlear lesion, and safety netting.
explain:
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL)

SSNHL is usually defined as a sensorineural loss of at least 30 dB over three contiguous frequencies developing within 72 hours. It is typically unilateral. Most cases remain idiopathic, but the first priority is to confirm that the loss is sensorineural rather than conductive, and to exclude dangerous mimics. It should be managed as urgent because earlier treatment is associated with better recovery.

Why the history matters

  • Central red flags: Vertigo with facial, limb, speech or visual symptoms may indicate a posterior circulation (for example AICA) stroke, which can present with sudden hearing loss. This patient has vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension).

  • Ototoxic drugs: Aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, platinum chemotherapy and high-dose salicylates should be identified.

  • Other triggers: Trauma, barotrauma, infection, noise and previous ear disease point to alternative causes or conductive loss.

  • Steroid safety: Diabetes, peptic ulcer disease and psychiatric history change the plan.

Bedside interpretation

Normal otoscopy makes wax, otitis and perforation unlikely. In a sensorineural loss the Weber lateralises to the better ear and the Rinne remains positive (air conduction better than bone conduction) on both sides. A conductive loss would lateralise to the affected ear with a negative Rinne on that side. Tuning forks are a screen only, so an audiogram is required.

Interpreting the audiogram and tympanometry

The audiogram confirms the bedside findings. The left air conduction thresholds are 40 to 70 dB, worse in the high frequencies, and the masked bone conduction thresholds sit within 5 dB of them, so there is no air-bone gap: the loss is sensorineural, not conductive. The left ear is more than 30 dB worse than the right over three or more contiguous frequencies, and with onset within 72 hours this meets the definition of SSNHL. Poor speech discrimination (64%) shows how much the loss affects her day to day and gives a baseline for recovery. Type A tympanograms confirm a normal middle ear. Her HbA1c of 7.4% matters because steroids will raise her glucose. The audiogram also provides the baseline for monitoring the response to treatment.

Investigations and why

  • Audiogram (pure-tone): confirms a sensorineural pattern and quantifies the loss. It also provides a baseline for monitoring treatment response.

  • MRI of the internal auditory canals: excludes a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma, which can present as SSNHL. Hearing may partly recover with steroids even when a lesion is present, so improvement does not exclude it. MRI should be arranged regardless of response, and it must not delay starting steroids.

  • Other tests (for example glucose, and bloods as directed by ENT) are guided by the clinical picture.

Management

  • Contact ENT the same day (local pathway) and arrange urgent audiology.

  • Start a corticosteroid promptly. Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily is usual, with caps that vary from 60 to 75 mg: the 2025 AJGP update suggests up to 70 mg daily for 7 days, then a taper over about a week; the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital guideline allows up to 75 mg; the US guideline gives up to 60 mg for 7 to 14 days. Follow the local guideline and ENT advice. For Mrs Halloran (72 kg) that is 60 to 72 mg daily, depending on the local cap. Intratympanic steroid is an ENT-led option for those who cannot take oral steroids or as salvage therapy.

  • In diabetes, warn about hyperglycaemia, arrange home glucose monitoring, and review early for medication adjustment.

  • Antibiotics and ear syringing have no role here.

  • Safety-net for stroke symptoms, vertigo and hearing loss in the other ear. Arrange follow-up with repeat audiogram and consider hearing rehabilitation if recovery is incomplete.

Communication

Acknowledge fears about stroke, tumour and deafness. Explain that MRI is both a safety check and part of the standard work-up, and address practical barriers such as claustrophobia. Explain that waiting over the weekend is not safe because earlier treatment gives a better chance of recovery. Be honest that many patients recover some or all of their hearing, but that the outcome cannot be guaranteed.
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. A high-performing candidate takes a structured history that screens for stroke red flags, ototoxic drugs and recent triggers, identifies diabetes as relevant to steroid use, and examines the ears, tuning forks, cranial nerves and balance. In Part 2 they read the audiogram as a left sensorineural loss with no air-bone gap that meets the definition of sudden sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with Weber to the right and a positive Rinne on both sides, and treat it as urgent: same-day ENT contact and oral steroids without waiting for imaging, with a diabetes plan. They explain clearly that MRI of the internal auditory canals is needed to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma, even if the hearing recovers, respond to her claustrophobia and her wish to wait, and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate recognises a sensorineural loss and offers steroids and ENT referral, but gives vague reasons for the MRI ("to see what is going on") and cannot explain why it is needed if steroids work. They may overlook ototoxic drugs, central red flags or the diabetes interaction, delay treatment until the scan, or accept the ear flush or antibiotic request.
patient:
Role: You are Jenny Halloran, a 52-year-old bookkeeper. You are anxious but cooperative. Speak in lay terms and ask the candidate to explain any jargon. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "My left ear is blocked and I can't hear properly out of it."

The hearing loss (give only when asked):

  • Onset: You woke two days ago (Wednesday) with the left ear sounding muffled, "like I have my head underwater". It was a bit worse by the end of that day and has not changed since. It does not come and go.
  • Severity: On the phone you cannot make out words in the left ear and have to swap ears. The right ear is normal.
  • Tinnitus and fullness: Constant high-pitched ringing in the left ear since waking, and a feeling of fullness.
  • Pain, discharge, itch: None.
  • Dizziness: No spinning. Yesterday you felt slightly unsteady when turning quickly, but this has settled. (Only reveal if asked about balance or dizziness.)
  • Red flags: No facial droop, limb weakness or numbness, speech or swallowing difficulty, double or blurred vision, or severe headache. No head injury.
  • Possible triggers: A cold with a blocked nose two weeks ago, now resolved. No flying, diving, straining or barotrauma. No loud noise exposure (you use earbuds on the train at moderate volume).
  • Self-treatment: Olive oil drops for two days, which did not help.
  • Previous episodes: Never had this before. No previous hearing problems, ear infections, ear surgery or hearing tests.

Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes for 6 years ("sugars are okay"). Hypertension. No stomach ulcers, no mental health history, no previous stroke or heart disease. Three years ago you had an MRI of your knee and panicked in the scanner; they had to stop and start again (only if asked about scans or small spaces). You have no pacemaker or metal implants (only if asked).

Medications: Metformin and candesartan (doses not known). Occasional paracetamol. No aminoglycoside antibiotics, frusemide, chemotherapy, aspirin or regular anti-inflammatories. No herbal remedies. Allergies: nil known. Vaccinations: up to date.

Family history: No hearing loss in the family. Your mother had a stroke at 75.

Social history: Lives with partner and teenage son. Non-smoker. Two standard drinks two or three nights a week. No recreational drugs. Walks occasionally.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: You think it is wax, or a blocked ear left over from the cold. You are worried it could be a stroke or a brain tumour, and that the hearing will not come back. You expect an ear flush or antibiotics.

Things to say: Early on: "I think it's just wax. Can't you just flush it out?" If there is time: "This isn't a stroke, is it?"
points: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time-critical: confirm with an audiogram, start steroids promptly (oral, or intratympanic via ENT, dose per local guideline) and involve ENT the same day.

MRI of the internal auditory canals is arranged to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma, and is still needed if hearing improves with steroids because improvement does not exclude a lesion.
Weber lateralising to the better ear with a positive Rinne on both sides indicates sensorineural loss; screen for stroke red flags and ototoxic drugs.
Diabetes alters steroid prescribing: warn about hyperglycaemia, plan glucose monitoring and arrange early review.

stem: You are a GP in a suburban general practice. Jenny Halloran, a 52-year-old bookkeeper, has come in on a Friday morning because she cannot hear properly in her left ear.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Halloran and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the results of an urgent audiogram and tympanometry done at the audiology clinic next door, and her recent blood tests. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including how you would explain it to Mrs Halloran and answer her questions, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Sudden hearing loss in one ear on waking

handover.model:
• Read: right thresholds 10 to 20 dB HL: normal. Left air conduction 40 to 70 dB HL, sloping down into the high frequencies (pure-tone average 54 dB HL), with masked bone conduction within 5 dB of air conduction at every frequency, so there is no air-bone gap: the loss is sensorineural. The left ear is 30 to 50 dB worse than the right at five contiguous frequencies (500 Hz to 8 kHz). Left speech discrimination is 64%.
  • For Mrs Halloran: a left sensorineural loss that came on over hours, meeting the definition of sudden sensorineural hearing loss (at least 30 dB over three contiguous frequencies within 72 hours). It agrees with Weber to the right and Rinne positive on both sides. Poor speech discrimination shows how much she has lost for everyday listening; discrimination worse than the thresholds predict raises suspicion of a retrocochlear cause, but the audiogram cannot tell cochlear from retrocochlear.
  • What it changes: treat as urgent: same-day ENT contact, oral prednisolone today without waiting for imaging, and MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. This audiogram is the baseline for the repeat audiogram that measures her recovery.

• Read: HbA1c 7.4% (57 mmol/mol), a little above the usual target of 7.0% or less. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine normal, eGFR 82, and no albuminuria.
  • For Mrs Halloran: type 2 diabetes that is reasonably but not tightly controlled, with normal kidney function. High-dose prednisolone will raise her glucose, mostly in the afternoon and evening; her BGL today is 8.2.
  • What it changes: diabetes is not a reason to withhold steroids, but it needs a plan: home glucose monitoring during the course, a clear threshold to call, and a review within a few days to adjust her treatment. Metformin can continue at this eGFR.

ask: What do the audiogram and tympanometry show, and how do they fit with your examination findings?
What is the most likely diagnosis, and what else must you consider?

What is your management approach? Mrs Halloran asks why she needs a scan of her head if the tablets might fix it, tells you she panicked in a scanner once, and asks whether steroid tablets are safe with her diabetes.
She asks: "Can I wait and see how it goes over the weekend? Will I get my hearing back?" What safety netting and follow-up will you arrange?
